summary:
What we developed: Earth Jukebox is a free web app that turns Earth science data into sound. Users pick a dataset (global temperature, Arctic sea ice, atmospheric CO₂ or sea level rise), then explore it two ways. Play through time glides a single tone through the years, with higher values giving a higher pitch. Scan the map sweeps across a world map for the chosen year, turning eight latitude bands into musical notes, with the north high and the south low. Each note’s loudness follows the local data value, so a shrinking Arctic ice cap fades the high notes. Every year also gets a plain-language text description, and the whole app works from the keyboard.

How it addresses the challenge: NASA’s Earth Information Center produces striking visualizations, but they reach people through sight alone. Earth Jukebox pairs visual map frames with sonifications generated in real time in the browser, so the same changes can be seen and heard. We also built a Python script and a file loader that convert rasters from NASA’s VEDA catalog, the platform behind the EIC dashboard, into the app’s data format. In this demo, the maps and values are illustrative and inspired by EIC themes, not NASA measurements.
details:
Earth Jukebox is a browser app that turns Earth science time series and maps into sound. A user picks a dataset (global temperature, Arctic sea ice, atmospheric CO₂, sea level rise, or their own loaded data file), then explores it two ways:

Play through time: a single tone glides as the years advance. Higher values give a higher pitch, and a soft tick marks each year.

Scan the map: a playhead sweeps west to east across a map of the chosen year. Eight latitude bands each play a pentatonic note, with the north high and the south low, and each note’s loudness follows the local data value. For example, as Arctic sea ice shrinks, the high notes fade.

Every year also gets a plain-language text description, and the whole app works from the keyboard (Space, arrow keys, S, and 1–4 for tracks), so it can be used without sight or a mouse. It offers light and dark themes.

We hope to widen who can engage with Earth science: blind and low-vision learners, people who learn by ear, and anyone who wants to feel a trend as well as see it.

Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Canvas API for the map frames, the Web Audio API for real-time synthesis, and a Python script (pystac-client, rasterio, numpy) that converts NASA raster data into the app’s data file
